meta.title: Nuxt vs Gatsby: Which one to choose in 2026? (features, performance & ecosystem & code compared)
meta.description: Compare Nuxt and Gatsby architectural trade-offs, rendering, routing, and data loading, and review side-by-side TypeScript to choose the right stack.

verdict: Choose Nuxt if you want one Vue-based framework that handles static sites, server rendering, hybrid rendering, and full-stack features like server routes and API endpoints. Choose Gatsby if you mainly need a React-based static site with a mature GraphQL data layer and a rich plugin ecosystem for content-heavy marketing sites. For most new projects in 2026, Nuxt's broader rendering flexibility makes it the safer default, but Gatsby remains a solid fit for established React teams with GraphQL-centric content pipelines.

comparison.category: Rendering modes and output flexibility. This criterion matters because it determines whether a single codebase can serve static pages, server-rendered pages, and client-rendered app sections.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt supports universal rendering, client-side rendering, static generation, and hybrid per-route rules, including server routes and API endpoints through Nitro. The exact behavior depends on the preset and hosting target you select, so teams should confirm which presets their platform supports before committing.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby is built around static site generation and produces pre-rendered HTML at build time, with client-side hydration and optional server-side rendering via Gatsby Functions and SSR support in recent versions. Some server-side capabilities require specific adapters or hosting configurations, so verify that your target host supports the features you need.

comparison.category: Data layer and content sourcing. Evaluation of how each tool fetches and unifies content from CMSs, APIs, files, and databases.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt does not impose a single data layer; it relies on composables and standard fetch patterns, with an official content module for Markdown and file-based content. This gives teams freedom to call any REST or GraphQL API, but it also means you own more of the integration and caching logic.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby's GraphQL data layer is a defining strength: it aggregates sources from many CMSs, files, and APIs into a unified schema queried at build time. The plugin ecosystem covers a large number of sources, though plugin maintenance and compatibility can vary by source, so check current plugin activity for your specific CMS.

comparison.category: Framework and ecosystem. Comparison of the underlying UI library, community size, and available modules.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt is built on Vue and benefits from the Vue ecosystem, including its module system, UI libraries, and composables conventions. The Nuxt ecosystem is active and includes first-party modules for common needs such as image optimization, content, and authentication, though the number of third-party modules can be smaller than what exists in React.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby is built on React and inherits the enormous React ecosystem for components, state management, and tooling. Its own plugin ecosystem is large, but it is more tightly scoped around data sourcing and build-time tasks, and some plugins age without frequent updates.

comparison.category: Performance and build workflow. How each framework handles build times, incremental builds, and client-side runtime behavior.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt uses Vite for development, which generally provides fast startup and hot module replacement, and Nuxt can route different pages to different rendering strategies for performance. Actual performance depends on configuration and hosting, so production measurements are essential.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby builds static pages ahead of time and supports incremental builds to reduce rebuild costs on large sites. Build times on content-heavy projects can still be significant, and runtime performance depends heavily on how much JavaScript ends up in the client bundle.

comparison.category: Full-stack capabilities. Whether the framework can handle server routes, authentication, and backend logic without a separate service.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt ships with Nitro, which supports server routes, API endpoints, middleware, and deploy presets for a wide range of hosting providers. This makes it practical to build full-stack applications, though teams should review security and data-access patterns for their chosen runtime.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby is primarily a static-site framework, with server-side capabilities added through Functions and SSR adapters. For applications that need substantial backend logic, you will typically pair Gatsby with a separate API or serverless service.

comparison.category: Learning curve and developer experience. How quickly developers can become productive and how much framework-specific knowledge is required.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt's conventions, auto-imports, and file-based routing make it approachable for developers who already know Vue, and its documentation is extensive. Developers new to Vue or to server rendering concepts will still need time to learn the framework's rendering model and deployment options.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby assumes familiarity with React and GraphQL, and its data layer adds a conceptual learning curve for newcomers. The documentation has improved over time, but the build-time data model and plugin configuration can be confusing for developers coming from simpler React setups.

comparison.category: Deployment and hosting compatibility. Which platforms and adapters each framework supports out of the box.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt's Nitro presets cover Node servers, serverless platforms, edge runtimes, and static hosting, so a single codebase can often be deployed to multiple targets. Availability of specific presets depends on the Nuxt version and your hosting provider, so verify support before planning an architecture.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby produces static assets that deploy to almost any static host, and its SSR and Functions features require compatible hosting or provider-specific adapters. Teams should confirm that their chosen host supports the specific Gatsby features they rely on.

comparison.category: Long-term maintenance and project fit. Assessment of how each framework fits projects with different lifecycle and staffing needs.
comparison.toolA: Nuxt is actively developed by its core team with regular releases, and it serves both content sites and application-style projects. Because it is a single framework for many rendering patterns, teams often avoid needing a second tool as requirements grow.
comparison.toolB: Gatsby remains maintained but is more narrowly positioned around static, content-driven sites, and its release cadence has slowed compared with earlier years. It is a reasonable choice for React teams with existing GraphQL content pipelines, but new projects should weigh the smaller scope of its roadmap.

faq.q: Which framework is better for a content-heavy marketing site in 2026?
faq.a: Gatsby is a strong fit for content-heavy marketing sites when your team is comfortable with React and GraphQL, because its data layer unifies many CMSs and files into one schema at build time. Nuxt is also a good choice and may be simpler if you prefer Vue or want the option to add server-rendered or hybrid pages later. For a purely static marketing site with a React team, Gatsby's content pipeline can save integration work; for a Vue team or a site that will grow into an application, Nuxt is usually the more flexible option.

faq.q: Can Nuxt and Gatsby both build fully static sites?
faq.a: Yes, both frameworks can generate static HTML that can be deployed to a CDN or static host. Nuxt offers static generation through its rendering modes and Nitro presets, while Gatsby is designed around static generation by default. The difference is that Nuxt can add server rendering or server routes within the same project when needed, whereas Gatsby's server-side features depend on specific adapters and hosting support.

faq.q: Which one has a better data layer for multiple CMS sources?
faq.a: Gatsby's GraphQL data layer is purpose-built for aggregating content from many sources, and its plugin ecosystem covers a wide range of CMSs and file types. Nuxt does not impose a data layer and instead relies on composables and standard fetch calls, which is flexible but requires you to build your own integration and caching patterns. If you have many content sources and a React team, Gatsby's approach can reduce boilerplate; if you want direct control over API calls, Nuxt is more straightforward.

faq.q: How do the two frameworks compare for full-stack applications?
faq.a: Nuxt has a clear advantage for full-stack work because Nitro provides server routes, API endpoints, and middleware within the same project. Gatsby is primarily a static-site framework, and while it offers Functions and SSR support through adapters, substantial backend logic usually requires a separate service. Teams building dashboards, authenticated apps, or dynamic APIs should generally evaluate Nuxt first, while static-first projects can stay with Gatsby.

faq.q: Is the learning curve significantly different between Nuxt and Gatsby?
faq.a: Both frameworks require learning their conventions, but the learning curve depends heavily on your existing skills. Developers who know Vue often find Nuxt approachable due to auto-imports, file-based routing, and clear documentation; developers who know React may find Gatsby's component model familiar, but the GraphQL data layer adds a separate concept to learn. If your team already knows Vue, Nuxt is usually faster to adopt; if your team is React-centric and already uses GraphQL, Gatsby may feel more natural.

faq.q: Which framework is a safer long-term choice for a new project?
faq.a: Nuxt is actively developed with a broad scope covering static, server-rendered, and hybrid applications, which makes it a safer default for projects whose requirements may evolve. Gatsby remains maintained and is a reasonable fit for static content sites within established React and GraphQL pipelines, but its narrower positioning means new projects should verify current feature support and roadmap activity. Neither choice is risk-free, so teams should confirm hosting compatibility, plugin maintenance, and version support before committing.

faq.q: Do both frameworks support server-side rendering?
faq.a: Nuxt supports server-side rendering as a first-class rendering mode, along with static generation and client-side rendering, and hybrid per-route rules are possible depending on configuration. Gatsby historically focused on static generation and has added SSR support that depends on specific adapters and hosting setups. If server rendering is central to your architecture, Nuxt offers a more direct path, while Gatsby teams should verify that their hosting provider supports the SSR features they need.

faq.q: Which framework should a small team with limited resources pick?
faq.a: For a small team, the decision usually comes down to existing skills and the desired hosting model. A Vue-focused team can use Nuxt to cover static pages, dynamic routes, and server endpoints in one project, potentially reducing infrastructure pieces to maintain. A React team with a simple static site and a CMS can use Gatsby and its plugins to minimize integration code. In both cases, confirm the long-term maintenance status of the plugins or modules you depend on before committing.
